items.title: Agent Distraction
items.summary: Analysis of over 913,000 coding agent sessions reveals that 13% expose agents to inline TODO(b/...) comments. items.title: Deleting or Extracting PDF Pages Without Uploading a 50MB File: How Browser /Pages Tree Copying Works
items.summary: If you need to drop two confidential pages from a 50MB legal contract or pull three sheets out of a scanned invoice bundle, uploading the entire file to a remote server just to reorder objects wastes bandwidth and exposes sensitive documents to third-party storage. A browser already has enough memory and compute to handle structural PDF edits locally. Editing pages inside the tab avoids network latency and keeps the file on your device. Under ISO 32000-1 (§7.7.3), a PDF stores its pages in a tree structure rooted in the document Catalog (/Root): Catalog (/Root) └── Pages Tree (/Pages) ├── Page 1 (/Page) -> Object 10 0 R ├── Page 2 (/Page) -> Object 15 0 R └── Page 3 (/Page) -> Object 20 0 R Each /Pages node holds two main entries: /Kids, an array of indirect references to child /Page objects or intermediate /Pages branch nodes, and /Count, an integer tracking the total number of leaf pages beneath that node. When a viewer opens a PDF, it reads the trailer at the end of the file, follows /Root to /Pages, and resolves individual page dictionaries on demand instead of decoding the entire document upfront. items.title: Understanding Promise.all(): failure, concurrency, and cancellation
items.summary: I used to think Promise.all() worked like a team where one person quitting cancels the whole project. One promise rejects, the rest stop, and Promise.all() reports the failure. That is a clean mental model, and it is wrong in the one way that matters. When a promise in Promise.all() rejects, the others do not stop. They keep running to completion, and Promise.all() just stops listening. I learned this the slow way, by watching a request I thought was cancelled finish anyway, and wondering where the extra work came from. Here is the rule, straight from MDN on Promise.all(): Promise.all() rejects immediately when any input promise rejects, and the rejection reason is the first promise that rejected. But rejecting the returned promise does not cancel the remaining operations. The other promises keep running, and their results are ignored. Subsequent rejections after the first are ignored too, so they do not even trigger unhandled rejection warnings. Say you fire three requests at once, user at 300ms, posts at 150ms, and prefs at 600ms, and posts fails. Promise.all() rejects at 150ms, the moment posts fails. items.title: Your UI should tell you what's going on
items.summary: I opened a budget app last month to check one number, how much I had left to spend, and I could not find it. The balance was on one screen, the spending was on another, and the budget was a third screen with a tiny progress bar I had to squint at. I knew the data was in there somewhere, the app had it, it just was not showing me. I closed it and did the math in my head instead, which is the exact moment a UI has failed at its job. I keep coming back to a line from Ben Halpern's post, ask more of your UI. The idea is simple: a UI should act like an instrument panel, showing you what is going on, live, instead of hiding the state behind taps and menus. A car dashboard does not make you open a menu to see your speed. It is just there, all the time, because the whole point of the dashboard is to tell you where you stand. I built a little budget tracker to try the idea out, nothing fancy, just a panel that shows the four things I actually check. Balance, spent this month against the budget, the next bill coming up, and whether the data is synced. Every number updates the moment something changes, so the panel is always current. items.title: How to convert decimal hours to hours and minutes
items.summary: Payroll systems and time trackers often store a workday as a decimal. Seven hours and forty-five minutes becomes 7.75. That's convenient for arithmetic: 7.75 plus 1.25 is exactly 9.0. It's less convenient when you have to print the same value as 7:45 on a timesheet. The conversion is short. The bugs I've run into are almost always in the same places: how you round a fractional minute, what you do with a negative adjustment, and whether a total over 24 hours should wrap like a clock or stay a duration. Treat the decimal as a duration, not a time of day. Multiply the decimal hours by 60 to get a total number of minutes. Round that total to an integer, using an explicit rounding rule. Split the integer with division and remainder: hours are the quotient, minutes are the remainder. So 7.75 × 60 = 465 minutes, and 465 ÷ 60 is 7 hours with 45 left over. Result: 7:45. The same steps work for a weekly total. 25.5 × 60 = 1,530 minutes, which is 25 hours and 30 minutes, not 1:30 the next morning. items.title: Base64 Is Not Encryption: A Practical Guide for Text and Small Files
items.summary: Base64 often appears in places that make it look more mysterious than it is: API payloads, email attachments, Data URLs, configuration files, and token segments. It is easy to mistake a long Base64 string for protected data. It is not protected. Base64 is an encoding that represents bytes with printable text characters. Anyone who has the value can decode it. That distinction matters when you are handling text, small files, or values that might contain secrets. Computers store data as bytes. Base64 groups three bytes, or 24 bits, then splits those bits into four groups of six. Each six-bit value becomes one character from a 64-character alphabet: ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZabcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz0123456789+/ For example, the UTF-8 bytes for cat become: cat -> Y2F0 The string Y2F0 looks different from cat, but it contains no secret. Decode it and the original bytes return immediately. RFC 4648 defines the standard Base64 alphabet, padding behavior, and the URL-safe variant used by many web formats. items.title: Balloon Payments in TypeScript: How to Keep the Final Balance Correct
items.summary: A balloon loan does not make part of the principal disappear. It moves it to the end of the schedule. That sounds obvious, but it leads to a surprisingly common implementation bug: code calculates a lower regular payment, then treats the balloon as if it were a separate expense that does not affect the amortization math. The result can be a schedule that looks plausible for 35 months and leaves the wrong balance in month 36. This article builds a monthly, fixed-rate balloon schedule in TypeScript. The model assumes payments occur at the end of each month, the annual rate remains fixed, and the balloon is due with the final regular payment. It does not cover taxes, insurance, refinancing approval, or lender-specific daily-interest and rounding rules. Use these variables: Variable Meaning P Amount financed, after any down payment r Monthly interest rate n Number of monthly payments B Balloon amount due in the final month C Regular monthly payment, excluding the balloon For months 1 through n - 1, the borrower pays C. items.title: Stripe webhook timed out? Return a 2xx first, then do the heavy work in a queue
items.summary: A webhook handler often does everything inside the request: verify the event, update the database, send the email, call another API, and only then answer. On a quiet day that finishes in time. On a busy one, or when a downstream service is slow, the response arrives late and Stripe's delivery log shows a timeout. This post covers what that status means, what Stripe says the handler should do first, how to move the slow part into a queue, and how to catch up on events that failed in the meantime. Every claim links to the doc it comes from (see Sources at the end). Open the webhook endpoint in the Stripe Dashboard and go to the Event deliveries tab. Stripe's docs describe it as a list of events and whether they're Delivered, Pending, or Failed, and clicking an event shows "the HTTP status code of the delivery attempt and the time of pending future deliveries." Look for the (Timed out) ERR status. Stripe's description: "The destination server took too long to respond to the webhook request." items.title: From API-First to AI-Native-First: How Should We Evolve Our Software Architecture?
items.summary: For years, we have been designing software systems around APIs. We expose REST endpoints, define gRPC contracts, implement business services, establish integration patterns and build applications that consume these capabilities. The API-first approach has served us well. It has enabled distributed systems, microservices, platform engineering and ecosystem integrations. But something fundamental is changing. AI is no longer just another feature that we integrate into an application. With the emergence of AI agents, applications are increasingly expected to understand context, discover capabilities, interact with external systems and execute business tasks. This raises an interesting architectural question: Are our existing applications ready to be consumed by AI agents, or are we going to keep building custom integrations every time we introduce a new AI use case? I believe we need to start thinking about an evolution towards AI-Native-First Software Architecture. Not by abandoning API-first architecture, but by extending it. items.title: Building Redaktix: A Zero-Server, Browser-Local PDF & Document Redaction Tool
items.summary: Last tax season, I needed to redact sensitive details from a W-2 form and a bank statement before sending them to a landlord. I tried several "free online redaction tools," but every single one required uploading my sensitive documents to an external server. That felt completely backwards for documents whose whole point is privacy. So I built Redaktix—a browser-local document redaction tool where your files never touch a server. 100% Client-Side: Everything runs locally inside the browser using HTML5 Canvas and WASM. Local OCR: Text extraction and pattern detection happen on-device inside a Web Worker. Auto-Detection: Uses regex and checksum algorithms (Luhn, ABA routing) to automatically detect US SSNs, bank numbers, credit cards, and EINs. Metadata & Layer Removal: Strips hidden PDF text layers and embedded metadata upon export, outputting a clean flattened PDF or image. Offline-Ready: Works as a PWA once loaded. You can try it live here: redaktix.com It's completely free to use. I'd love your feedback on the client-side redaction approach, UX, and detection accuracy on real-world scanned documents!

items.title: One Chromium per screenshot, or one shared browser? Time, memory and leaks measured in Playwright
items.summary: A service that takes screenshots on request has to decide what one request owns: a whole Chromium, a browser context inside a shared Chromium, or just a page inside a shared context. I measured the three on one machine, then measured what each choice leaks when it goes wrong. Short version of what I found: sharing a browser saved about half a second per job when jobs ran one at a time, and about 240 MiB at concurrency 2. The bigger differences were isolation and cleanup. A forgotten context.close() cost about 105 MiB per job and took the browser from 230 MiB to 6.6 GB in 60 jobs. Everything ran on 2026-11-11: Linux 6.8, 6 cores, Node v24.22.2, Playwright 1.63.0 with the bundled chrome-headless-shell (Chrome for Testing 153.0.8010.12). The machine also runs other services, so load average was 2 to 3 and absolute times are slow. Compare the rows with each other, not with your laptop. Only the headless shell was tested, only on Linux, only against a local fixture server. Each job opens a page with 12 SVG images (served by a local server with a 40 ms delay each), 200 paragraphs of text, waits for load, takes a full-page 1280 px wide screenshot and closes what it owns. 24 jobs per run.

items.title: I run 38 PDF tools with no server. Here is where the work went instead.
items.summary: When you merge two PDFs on most websites, your files go to someone's server, get processed there, and come back. I built PDFRoll the other way around: 38 tools, static pages, and nothing that processes a file anywhere but in your own browser tab. That sounds like a privacy feature, and it is. But it is mostly an architecture decision, and it moved the hard problems to places I did not expect. This post is about those places. The site is static HTML on a CDN. The PDF work is done by libraries shipped to the browser: pdf-lib to create and rewrite PDFs PDF.js to read and render them qpdf compiled to WebAssembly for encryption and password removal Tesseract (WebAssembly again) for OCR libheif for iPhone photos, plus a few converters for Word, Excel and PowerPoint files The only thing a visitor's browser ever sends to my side is a counter. More on that below, because what it is allowed to count turned out to matter. Those libraries add up to megabytes. If a page loaded them all, the person who came to rotate one page would pay for an OCR engine. So nothing heavy loads with the page. items.summary: I built a small static scanner for MCP servers after I found a real SSRF bug in one of my own webhook routes. Then I ran it on 36 public MCP servers to see how bad the ecosystem looked. First result: 482 findings. Second result, after I read them: almost none were real. e2e and test helpers that call exec() on purpose db.exec() and RegExp.exec(), which share a name with child_process.exec but have nothing to do with it strings and comments that contain "http://" or a secret-looking token placeholder keys like sk_test_xxx in READMEs and examples Skip test, e2e and scripts directories (opt back in with --include-tests) Flag SSRF only when the caller controls the host of the URL, not just a path or query Ignore matches inside strings and comments Flag exec-injection only for child_process and new Function Filter placeholder secrets Same 36 repos after the fix: 28 findings. I read all of them. They are shell strings that interpolate paths or dates. None are exploitable as far as I can tell, and I did not find anything worth disclosing. items.title: Exchange Rate API Unit Testing: Mocks, Fixtures and Contract Tests
items.summary: Code that depends on live FX is awkward to test. The rate changes every minute, the network may be down in CI, and a test that asserts 0.9215 passes today and fails tomorrow. This guide shows how to test exchange rate API code properly: inject a rate provider, use fixtures with the real response shape, mock HTTP in Vitest or Jest with msw and in Python with responses, cover the 401 and 429 paths, and run one contract test against the real API every night. A test that calls the real API and checks a number is not a test. It is a coin toss with a delay. Split the work in two: Unit tests run offline with frozen rates. They check your logic: rounding, cross rates, caching, error handling. A contract test runs on a schedule against the real API. It checks that the response still has the shape your code expects. The easiest code to test never calls fetch from business logic. It depends on an interface, and the HTTP client is one implementation of it. // rates.ts export interface RateProvider { getRate(source: string, target: string): Promise ; } export class RateError extends Error { constructor(public code: string, public status: number, public resetsAt?: string | null) { super(code); }

items.title: Free Currency Converter API for iOS and Android: Swift and Kotlin
items.summary: A free currency converter API is easy to call from a mobile app. Doing it well takes three more things: the app must work offline with the last known rates, it must tell the user how old those rates are, and the API key must not be inside the app binary. This guide covers all three, with working code for iOS in Swift and Android in Kotlin. The examples use the AllRatesToday rates endpoint, which returns mid-market rates for 160+ currencies, refreshed every 60 seconds. An iOS or Android app is a file the user downloads. Anything compiled into it, including an API key in Info.plist, BuildConfig or an obfuscated string, can be extracted with free tools in minutes. Once extracted, the key works from anywhere until you rotate it. So the app never talks to the rates API directly: The app calls https://rates.example.com/rates?source=USD&target=EUR,GBP,JPY on your own backend. The backend adds Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY, calls AllRatesToday, caches the answer and returns the same JSON array. items.title: Content-addressed keys for transformed images in object storage
items.summary: Name every transformed image after what made it: a SHA-256 of the source bytes, plus a hash of the canonical options and the encoder version. The same input then always lands on the same object key, so a cache check is one read. On my Mac a repeat 640 px AVIF from a 9.8 MB camera JPEG dropped from 296.9 ms to 5.1 ms. A URL names where an image came from, not what it is. Two users upload the same IMG_0001.jpg with different pixels. One user uploads the same photo twice under two names. A key built from the name gets the first case wrong and misses the second. A key built from the bytes gets both right. Identical bytes share one hash. Different bytes never do, in any practical sense. The options matter just as much. A 640 px AVIF at quality 50 is a different object from a 1200 px WebP of the same photo. So the key has two halves: the source and the recipe. Three things: The source hash. SHA-256 of the uploaded bytes, before any decode. The canonical options. Width, format, quality, and anything else that changes the output, serialized with sorted keys. The encoder version. A sharp or libvips upgrade can change the bytes it writes. items.summary: I run many Claude Code sessions on one machine at the same time, often ten or more. Each of them makes a shell call every few seconds, and every shell call goes through the PreToolUse hooks of claude-bulkhead, the plugin I wrote to stop those sessions from killing each other's dev servers, taking each other's ports and committing each other's half-finished edits. This post is about what those hooks cost, why the cost grew with the number of sessions, and how version 0.3.0 changed it. Up to version 0.2, bulkhead registered seven separate Bash hooks: kill-guard, wait-guard, memory-guard, port-guard, checkout-guard, disk-guard and basics. Claude Code runs every matching hook for a tool call side by side, each as its own process with the payload on stdin. On an idle machine that looks cheap. The guards run in parallel, most of them only look at the command text, and one call took 47 ms on my MacBook Pro (M5 Pro, Node 24). The number that mattered was a different one. Starting Node alone takes 32 ms on that machine, so every guard paid most of its cost before reading a single byte of input. Seven guards meant seven Node processes per shell call. items.title: The __proto__ Key in an API Response Is a Merge Bug Waiting to Happen
items.summary: Every JSON formatter shows it plainly: a key named __proto__ sitting in the middle of an otherwise normal API response. It looks harmless because nothing crashes. That is exactly the problem — the bug shows up two files later, in the code that copies the object. I tested this in Node 22 with one payload: {"__proto__":{"polluted":"yes"},"ok":1} JSON.parse() itself is safe. The key becomes an ordinary own property: const obj = JSON.parse(raw); Object.keys(obj); // [ '__proto__', 'ok' ] obj.polluted; // undefined obj.hasOwnProperty('__proto__'); // true So parsing is not the vulnerability. Copying is. const merged = Object.assign({}, obj); merged.polluted; // 'yes' — inherited from the attacker's object ({}).polluted; // undefined — the global prototype is still intact Object.assign performs a [[Set]], and __proto__ is an accessor defined on Object.prototype, so the target's prototype is replaced. One object is compromised. A recursive merge is worse: function merge(target, source) { for (const k in source) { if (source[k] && typeof source[k] === 'object') { target[k] = target[k] || {}; merge(target[k], source[k]); } else target[k] = source[k]; } return target; } merge({}, obj); ({}).

items.title: I built a 30-second blind audio quiz web app to settle music debates
items.summary: I wanted a fast way to test whether my friends actually recognize tracks quickly instead of guessing from lyrics or text questions. So I built SonicPulse, a mobile-first audio quiz you can play directly in the browser without creating an account. Pick an artist or swipe through genre decks Listen to a 30-second audio preview against a countdown clock Pick the matching track from four choices across 10 rounds Instant guest mode by default, with optional Google sign-in for score history Try it out here: https://sonicpulse-sable.vercel.app The frontend uses React, Vite, Tailwind CSS, and Framer Motion, backed by a Flask API and Supabase. Two tricky bugs I had to sort out for mobile testers were handling 100dvh viewport heights smoothly and letting users tap anywhere on the audio player card to unlock audio on mobile Safari. If you try it on your phone, I would appreciate honest feedback on loading speed, audio delay, or any layout issues.

items.summary: A compiler that refuses a contract that says too little This article was written with the help of an AI assistant (Claude), like the language it describes, which was built with Claude Code. I checked every figure against the repository and I take responsibility for the content. It follows Green proofs, empty promises. In my previous article I asked a small model to write verified Dafny. The proofs were green. But 5 of the 8 contracts barely constrained the result: a length, a format, a shape. One of those methods was wrong, and the proof did not notice. A verifier proves what it is asked to prove. If the same agent writes the code and its contract, it can ask for exactly as much as it manages to prove. Checking the proof is not enough; the question is whether the contract says enough. items.summary: I found it by reading a send log, not a page. Dozens of "The fire is lit" emails had gone out at 8pm, and an hour later the daily counter on our Resend account read 97 of 100. Three sign-in codes were left for the rest of the day, during the one hour people were actually trying to log in. Fyreflock is a random video and text chat app. It runs a feature I'd nicknamed the campfire: the matching queue only opens in set evening windows, and if you'd asked to be told when it opens, we'd email you. Turns out that email and the one carrying your sign-in code were drawing from the same tap, and nobody had told the tap it had two jobs. Resend's free plan gives you 100 sends a day. items.title: How NewsNinja syncs all your data in less than 1 MB of iCloud
items.summary: NewsNinja is an RSS reader for iPhone, iPad, Mac, and Vision Pro that I build after hours. This post was originally published on the NewsNinja blog. NewsNinja has no account and no sync server, but it still syncs between your iPhone, iPad, Vision Pro, and Mac. Your feeds, categories, settings, read articles, and starred articles all go through a single, small Apple API: NSUbiquitousKeyValueStore, the iCloud key-value store. The whole thing fits in less than 1 MB. This post explains how the store works, why I picked it, and the tricks that keep NewsNinja inside its limits as the app has grown. The first version of NewsNinja was a very simple RSS reader. The only thing that needed to sync was the list of feeds you subscribed to, and a feed list is just a list of URLs. For that, a real database felt like overkill. Core Data or SwiftData would have meant a schema, a model container, migrations, and a CloudKit container to set up and maintain, all to store an array of strings. I didn't want to run my own sync server either. NewsNinja doesn't have accounts, and I wanted to keep it that way. NSUbiquitousKeyValueStore was exactly the right size for the problem. items.title: I Built a State Management Library That Works Like React's useState
items.summary: I Built a State Management Library That Works Like React's useState — Meet CreateStore If you've worked with React, you've probably used useState countless times. It's simple, predictable, and gets the job done. But as an application grows, things get a little more complicated. You have components deeply nested in the component tree that need access to the same state. Suddenly, you're passing props through multiple components, introducing Context Providers, or bringing in a state management library with its own concepts and boilerplate. I kept thinking: Why can't sharing global state be as simple as using useState? That question led me to build CreateStore, a JavaScript state management library that I've recently published on npm. In this article, I'll walk through the problem, how CreateStore approaches it, and how you can start using it in a React application. Let's say we're building a simple todo application. We have two components: TodoCount – displays the number of todos. AddTodo – allows users to add new todos. items.title: Next.js opengraph-image in Crawled – currently not indexed: should you fix it?
items.summary: Search Console's Page indexing report put 14 URLs from this site under "Crawled – currently not indexed". Only 4 of them were pages. The other 10 were files: six per-page opengraph-image routes, feed.xml, favicon.ico, and the root card twice, once with its cache-busting query. None of those should ever be in the index, so the status is harmless for them. I still added X-Robots-Tag: noindex to every one, but the more useful thing I learned is what that header does not do. In the App Router, an opengraph-image.tsx file next to a page becomes a route that returns a PNG, and Next.js writes its URL into the page's head: Googlebot follows URLs it finds, and this is a plain absolute URL on your own domain. It fetches the image, sees that it isn't a page, and doesn't index it as one. Search Console reports that outcome as "Crawled – currently not indexed". That label covers "we looked and passed", and for a social card that is the right result. So if the only rows in that bucket are image routes, feeds and icons, nothing is broken. I tried researching first through DDG and Google, but (and I recognize this might be a skill issue) most things I found are either SEO slop or trying to sell/market some service. For some more context and to give a concrete example as to what I'm interested in, I got my hands on a Raspberry Pi which I'd like to use to start tinkering with self-hosting. My main goal would be to host my (static) website on it, potentially adding more things in the future. Some people I asked this question recommended solutions like Cloudflare Tunnels to make it secure, but using such a provider almost feels like it defeats the point of self-hosting, so I'm curious whether it's viable to do it using open source tooling, any gotchas one might encounter, and generally any thoughts you might have on the topic. items.title: From idea to the App Store in a weekend: a medication reminder built in November 2026
items.summary: On Thursday evening at 20:40 I opened an empty folder with a short note: remind me to take my pills, let me confirm I took them, keep a history, count what is left at home. On Friday at about 16:00 the app was submitted to App Store review, for iPhone, iPad and Mac, in four languages. On Monday morning Apple approved it. The app is Vzato ("taken" in Czech), and it is in the App Store now. It is free, open source under MPL-2.0, has no server and no accounts, and syncs through the user's own iCloud. The code is on GitHub. I built it with Claude Code. This post is about what that looked like in practice: why I built it, how the day went, what I did and what the AI did, and what it means to write and ship an app like this now. It wasn't magic, and it wasn't a toy either. There are plenty of them. I tried several before this, and none of them worked for me. Some I did not like. Some I simply did not understand how to use. And most of them missed small things that matter a lot when you actually take pills every day: When can I eat? Some medication has to be taken on an empty stomach, 30 minutes before food. So the reminder I need is not only "take your pill", it is also "you can eat now"

items.summary: Flattening a comment thread into a single array works until you need to reply to a reply. Then you're faking depth with parent ids, and every edit or delete means rebuilding the whole list. Build a threaded comments UI: render a recursive thread, then reply, edit, collapse, and delete nodes while every update returns a new tree instead of mutating the seed. 👉 https://www.reactchallenges.com/challenges/nested-comments Render the full thread from initialComments, with replies nested inside their parent. Each comment shows its author and text, and exposes reply, edit, and delete controls. Comments with replies get a collapse control with aria-expanded that hides or shows only their replies. items.title: Return or throw? Result pattern vs exceptions in ASP.NET Core
items.summary: The order does not exist. Now what? Every .NET API answers this question many times a day, and there are two camps. One throws a NotFoundException and lets something upstream turn it into a 404. The other returns the error as a value. Both work. Both have real costs. This post lists the pros and cons of each, shows numbers, and ends with the rule I use. TL;DR Return the errors a caller can expect: not found, conflict, validation failed. They are 4xx. Throw what should never happen: a bug, a dead database. It is a 500. You need both, and both should produce the same error shape. public async Task GetAsync(int id, CancellationToken ct) { var order = await repo.FindAsync(id, ct) ?? throw new NotFoundException($"Order {id} does not exist."); return order.ToDto(); } Somewhere else, an IExceptionHandler or a middleware catches NotFoundException and writes the 404. It is built in. Every .NET developer knows it and every library already uses it. The happy path stays clean. There are no checks after each call. It cannot be ignored by accident. items.title: Vertical Japanese broke my OCR: how I group manga text into speech bubbles on iOS
items.summary: Point a general camera translator at a page of raw manga and you get one of two results. A single paragraph of English in an order that makes no sense, or one tiny box per column of text, each translated on its own, so nothing reads like a sentence. I build Yomi, an iOS app for reading manga that only exists in Japanese, and most of the work turned out not to be translation at all. It was geometry: deciding which pieces of text belong to the same speech bubble, in what order to read them, and where to put the English afterwards. This post is about that part. Three things a sign or a menu never does to you: Vertical text. Japanese bubbles are usually written in columns, top to bottom, and the columns read right to left. OCR engines tend to return each column as its own line. Many separate blocks. A page has eight to fifteen bubbles. A translator that treats the page as one block of text merges dialogue from different characters. Small text at page scale. A whole page photographed by a phone leaves each glyph a few pixels wide. items.summary: Most free document scanners upload your pages to a server for text recognition. Passports, tax forms and receipts included. There's no technical need for that on a modern phone, so I built LumenScan as an experiment in doing all of it locally. This is how it's put together. Capture: VNDocumentCameraViewController from VisionKit, the same component Apple Notes uses. You get live edge detection, auto-capture, multi-page flow and a corner editor for free. I first wrote a custom AVFoundation camera, then dropped it as the main path; it now only runs on simulators or devices without Apple's scanner. OCR: the Vision framework's text recognition, on device. I set it up to cover English plus Hindi, Tamil and Telugu, since the first target market was India. PDF: PDFKit builds the output and handles annotation and signing. The recognized text is laid under the page image so the PDF is searchable. History: SwiftData. items.title: Why a plain FFT tuner locks onto the wrong note, and what I used instead (McLeod Pitch Method on iOS)
items.summary: I'm a solo developer at a small studio, and I recently shipped a guitar tuner and metronome called Maestro. The tuner was the part I got wrong first, so this post is about that. The obvious way to build a tuner: take a window of microphone samples, run an FFT, pick the tallest peak, convert to a note. It works on a sine wave. On a real guitar it doesn't, because the loudest bin is often the 2nd or 3rd harmonic, not the fundamental. A low E (about 82 Hz) will happily read as the E an octave up, or as a B, depending on the pluck. MPM computes a normalized square-difference autocorrelation of the window. Instead of looking for the biggest peak in frequency space, it looks for repeating structure in time, and normalizes by signal energy at each lag so quiet tails don't lose to loud attacks. Then it picks the first strong peak, which is the fundamental, and refines it with parabolic interpolation for sub-sample precision (this is what gets you to a fraction of a cent). A few practical details from the implementation: Range: roughly 30 Hz to 2 kHz, so a 5-string bass low B and a violin's top register both fit. items.title: Open Core in a Public Repo: Gate Paid Features With License Keys, Not Secrecy
items.summary: Your repository is public. Anyone can read the paid modules, fork them, and build them. So what actually separates the Community edition from the paid one? In open core and Fair Source projects the answer is not code secrecy. It is the license key: a signed entitlement that tells one self-hosted installation which paid features it is allowed to use. This post walks through how to design that boundary so it stays fair to operators and practical for you. Classic open core keeps the core under an open source license and puts commercial modules in a separate directory (often ee/) with their own terms. Fair Source goes a step further: the commercial code is readable, but the license limits certain uses of current versions and converts to a permissive license later. Keygen moved to FCL, and Directus announced an FCL-derived license for v12 together with registration keys for paid users. items.title: Building a Thread-Safe Concurrent List in C# from Scratch
items.summary: While .NET provides powerful thread-safe collections in the System.Collections.Concurrent namespace—such as ConcurrentDictionary and ConcurrentQueue —it notably lacks a built-in ConcurrentList . If you have ever needed to read and write to a list from multiple background threads simultaneously, you quickly realize that standard collections like List fall apart under concurrent pressure. In this article, we will build a custom, production-grade ConcurrentList from scratch in C# using ReaderWriterLockSlim, explore why dynamic lists are chosen over fixed arrays, test it with a multithreaded stress test, and analyze the performance costs involved. When multiple threads read and write to a standard List concurrently, several issues arise: Data Corruption: Interleaved writes corrupt internal array capacity tracking and element pointers. Race Conditions: Two threads inserting at the same index simultaneously will overwrite one another, resulting in lost data. Exceptions: Modifying a collection while another thread is iterating over it throws an InvalidOperationException. items.title: 800 MB of Arrays Nobody Asked For
items.summary: I was profiling a request handler last week and the gen0 line on the allocation chart kept ticking up on a path that, as far as I could tell, allocated nothing. No LINQ, no string building, nothing getting new-ed up. Just a little helper I'd written to pick the largest of a few timeout values, something like PickTimeout(configTimeout, retryTimeout, defaultTimeout). The helper took params int[]. That was the whole problem. Here's the thing I'd managed to forget: every time you call a params method with loose arguments, the compiler builds an array to carry them. PickTimeout(a, b, c) quietly compiles to PickTimeout(new[] { a, b, c }). One array per call. On a path that runs a handful of times per request, that's nothing you'll ever notice. Mine sat inside a per-row loop, so it ran a lot. So I did what I always do when a number smells wrong: boiled it down to the dumbest benchmark that still shows the effect and ran it. Pick the max of three ints, twenty million times, count the bytes. static int MaxOfArray(params int[] values) { int max = int.MinValue; foreach (int v in values) if (v > max) max = v; return max; } The result wasn't subtle. params int[] : 800,000,040 bytes gen0= 5 335

items.title: My IEnumerable Parameter Boxed 80 MB. PGO Clawed Back 85%.
items.summary: I had a helper that summed a column of ints. Tiny method, the kind you write without thinking. I'd typed its parameter as IEnumerable out of pure habit, the "accept the most general thing you can" reflex that every C# tutorial drills into you. Months later it turned up near the top of an allocation trace, and I stared at it for a while because there's no new anywhere in it. It's a foreach and a +=. What could it possibly be allocating? The allocation wasn't in my code. It was hiding in the foreach. static long SumConcrete(List items) { long total = 0; foreach (var x in items) total += x; return total; } static long SumInterface(IEnumerable items) { long total = 0; foreach (var x in items) total += x; return total; } Same body, character for character. The only thing that differs is the parameter type, and that one difference decides whether the enumerator the foreach grabs lives on the stack or on the heap. Here's why. List .GetEnumerator() returns List .Enumerator, which is a struct. When you foreach over a concrete List , the compiler binds straight to that struct method and the enumerator never leaves the stack. Corrections are very welcome! An actor is a reference type that protects its own mutable state. Only one task runs on an actor at a time, so the compiler can prove there are no data races. Code outside the actor has to await to reach that state. enum BankError: Error { case insufficientFunds } actor BankAccount { private(set) var balance: Decimal = 0 func deposit(_ amount: Decimal) { balance += amount } func withdraw(_ amount: Decimal) throws { guard balance >= amount else { throw BankError.insufficientFunds } balance -= amount } } let account = BankAccount() await account.deposit(100) let current = await account.balance Inside the actor, calls are synchronous. There's no await between the guard and balance -= amount, so that check-then-update can't be interrupted. Actors are reentrant. items.title: Loading 100 Photos from PHPicker Without Freezing: Order, Progress and Cancellation in Swift
items.summary: Someone selects 80 photos in the system picker, taps Add, and your app goes quiet. No spinner, no count, just a frozen sheet while the item providers grind through iCloud downloads in whatever order they finish. When the results finally arrive, photo 37 is in slot 2, two files are missing, and nobody knows why. PHPickerViewController is the right tool for picking photos on iOS: no full library permission, the system handles the UI, and it supports multi-select. But the part after picker(_:didFinishPicking:) is all yours, and that is where batch apps tend to go wrong. items.summary: If your iOS app offers Sign in with Apple, Apple asks you to revoke the person's token when they delete their account. With Supabase that's awkward: native sign-in uses signInWithIdToken, so you never receive an Apple refresh token, and at deletion time you have nothing to revoke. Here's an approach that works without storing anything from Apple. When the person taps Delete Account, show the Sign in with Apple sheet once more. It returns a fresh authorization code, valid for five minutes and usable once. Send that code to a Supabase Edge Function. Officially, you are switching between "two of America's fastest 5G networks." Fi Wireless does note that users have top priority, so data is never deprioritized on the Primary network. Meanwhile, there's "highest QCI priority" on the backup network that means subscribers are among the last to be slowed down when there's congestion. This is also available internationally when local partner networks are available with the Flexible and Unlimited Premium plans. Blender 5.3 also brings support for NVIDIA RTX Spark devices. For the Cycles code in Blender 5.3 the Principled BSDF for shader nodes now supports dispersion. Another notable change with Blender 5.3 is the Vulkan back-end now being the default on Windows (except for Windows on ARM) and Linux systems. items.summary: An anonymous reader quotes a report from NBC News: The Food and Drug Administration said Monday that GLP-1 drugmakers must add a warning label about a rare eye condition that can cause sudden blindness. The condition, called nonarteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy, or NAION, affects the optic nerve, which carries signals from the eye to the brain. When blood flow to the nerve is reduced or blocked, it can cause sudden vision loss. The condition is permanent with no known treatment. The FDA said "there is a potential increased risk of rare NAION" in people taking GLP-1 drugs. The agency's requirement applies to all GLP-1s, including Novo Nordisk's Ozempic and Wegovy and Eli Lilly's Mounjaro and Zepbound, as well as several older GLP-1 diabetes medications. [...] Previous research has found that GLP-1 use may increase the risk of NAION, and Lilly has said it was aware of studies on the potential link. The FDA said it began looking into a possible link after a 2024 study published in JAMA Ophthalmology that found diabetes patients prescribed semaglutide were four times as likely to develop NAION as those not prescribed the drug. items.title: Elon Musk’s nearly half a billion dollars in midterms spending was a flop
items.summary: The tech billionaire set spending record as he poured $446m into campaigns for failed Republican candidates Elon Musk set a record for election spending this year after pouring nearly half a billion dollars into backing Republicans in the US midterm elections. It turned out to be a poor investment. The SpaceX and Tesla CEO contributed at least $446m to Republican-aligned Super Pacs and groups over the course of the elections, specifically targeting several key Senate races in an effort to help the Trump administration retain Republican control of Congress. He outdid his own 2024 spending of nearly $290m. Yet as Democrats swept to power across the country on Tuesday night, it became clear that Musk would get nearly nothing in return for his hundreds of millions in spending. Continue reading...

items.title: How to Train a Swarm (19 minute read)
items.summary: Swarms are AI systems where multiple agents cooperate towards a shared goal. This post discusses a technique called collective inference-time scaling, where agents scale the amount of useful work performed in parallel and the communication needed to achieve it. It also explains how to design incentives for parallel work, and covers the general topic of designing incentives for reinforcement learning.

items.title: Why Agents Are Soon Only Going to Have 1 Tool (9 minute read)
items.summary: Agents are collapsing their entire tool catalog into one 'exec' tool. This allows models to write short scripts that chain, combine, and await actions inside isolated sandboxes. Models can now reliably combine and chain dependent actions in a single pass. In the previous standard tool-calling model, agents could only perform single actions, but the exec tool allows them to perform multiple actions.

items.title: Poisoning 0.1% of pretraining data planted a remote-code backdoor in a coding agent (78 minute read)

The backdoor grew stronger with model size and still fired at a 0.0005% poison rate.
